title: Touring Japan with the band and its reception
summary: Green travels with the band, with concerts in Tokyo and Osaka, packed halls, and George's love of Japan.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Did you hear the George Lewis band playing in Japan? All the time. I traveled with them.
All the time. I traveled with them.

Beautifully. The first concert was at the Great Music Hall in Tokyo, which seems to be about the size of the Radio City Music Hall in New York. Absolutely crowded. Plush seats. You can't out nightclub the Japanese. This wasn't a nightclub. Just a huge theater. Huge balcony. Every seat taken. It seems some union in Japan was sponsoring this tour for their members. People interested in music, I think, could pay a certain fee and be invited to a certain number of concerts a year. This was one of the concerts on the list. And here was this audience, many of them I don't think knowing what to expect, although we later found out that many of the men who, Japanese, who appeared in the swing coffee shop that first night turned out to be Japanese musicians that we've become very friendly with since, who were in the neighborhood, gotten on the phone. And the band was just beautifully received. There was a big sign over the stage, George Lewis. I forget the first, but they played Alexander's Ragtime Band. And the last tune was Till We Meet Again with George, thanking them all for being there. And the young Japanese girls coming up with flowers and giving it to them. And the band just beautifully received.
Did you hear them in the Osaka? What was it?

Then, then there were several concerts in Tokyo. Then went to Osaka, to the Shin-Ozaka Hotel, where the band stayed and I stayed too. And there was a music hall around the corner. Again, absolutely huge, very plush. And now a fantastically enthusiastic response because Osaka was the center of the Japanese, the Dixieland Rascals, the Japanese band. And it was a fantastic And it was just mobbed. And terribly successful. And in the lobby of the hotel, there was a great chance for the Japanese to get to know the American musicians. Papa John, Joseph at 89, sitting there, either talking to a young, a Japanese infant or an elderly Japanese man. Neither speaking the other's language, but understanding each other perfectly for hours on end.

I believe they played in a soccer, but I think Jaffee said they played for something like 40 nights in a row. Yep. Is that right? He said that they were actually, that the festival hall where it was there, and they were actually packed out more every night.
Every night, 40 nights, I think roughly is correct. That is really extraordinary. Absolutely packed.
It's hard to imagine that happening in any city in the world. Yeah. So, what did George think of Japan? Did you ever hear him talking about it?

He loved it. He loved it. He loved the people of, I think the words that he, one of the records, George Lewis in Japan, his closing salutation to them or saying goodbye to them, I think it's completely honest, the lovely people of Japan. He was so pleased. He recognized fully their appreciation of what he was doing. Yes. And he responded to it. And all the musicians do. And Joe Watkins to this day still talks of Japan. He and Manny Sales and I bummed around together sometimes if we had an off evening and explored the little bars and pubs and they just loved it. Just loved it.
